The SPPT noted that members felt these disparate approaches were “fragmented, confusing, and difficult to administer.” SPP used power flow modeling to support the establishment and application of voltage thresholds for cost allocation (SPP 2010c). The resulting Highway/Byway method allocates 100% of costs for facilities greater than 300 kV to the region on a load ratio share basis. For lower-voltage lines greater than 100 kV, one-third of costs are allocated regionally on a load ratio share basis, and two-thirds are allocated to the local transmission-owner zone where the facility is located. Facilities less than 100 kV are cost allocated 100% to local zones (Table 5). Table 5. SPP currently estimates there are 489 projects identified through its Integrated Transmission Planning process and subject to Highway/Byway cost allocation in its active portfolio, accounting for more than 88% of the total portfolio budget (SPP 2025b). 3.2.4 PJM Artificial Island Project The PJM Artificial Island Project provides an example of the challenges to using detailed power system modeling for cost allocation. The $266.5 million Artificial Island Project was proposed in 2015 to resolve the stability issues identified by PJM at the Salem and Hope Creek nuclear plants in New Jersey and to relieve congestion on the Delmarva Peninsula (PJM 2015a). The project consisted of 12 transmission enhancements—5 would operate above a threshold of a 500-kV or 345-kV double circuit, and the remaining 7 were planned below this threshold, including a 3-mile 230-kV underwater cable beneath the Delaware River (Figure 8). These projects were the first to be planned under PJM’s Order 1000 transmission tariff as part of the Regional Transmission Expansion Planning process (PJM Inside Lines 2021). 17 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Under the tariff, the costs for facilities greater than 500 kV or double-circuit 345 kV are allocated 50% across the region based on load ratio share and 50% using a method called distribution factor analysis, or DFAX (PJM 2010). The DFAX method determine cost allocations based on simulated power flows over a new transmission line to customer zones using hourly production cost simulations of network operations for the existing system with the added transmission upgrade (PJM 2024). For lower- voltage facilities—defined as facilities operating below 500 kV, or below 345 kV in the case of double-circuit 345-kV lines—100% of costs are allocated using the DFAX method.
